author: ROAPE
title: The sports commercializers are in town
content:
Two recent stories from Kenya reflect the rapid growth, rising ambitions, and increasing commercialization and professionalization of East Africa’s sports sector.




In the first, Helios Sports and Entertainment Group, a private equity firm focused on the continent, teamed up with Zaria Group, fronted by former NBA executive 

Masai Ujiri

, to build a $294 million sports and entertainment hub in Nairobi. Then, Oscar-winning actress Lupita Nyong’o 

announced

 she was investing in Nairobi City Thunder, which plays in the Basketball Africa League (BAL).




A few days later, reports said Nyong’o’s investment in Nairobi City Thunder may kickstart further investment in the BAL and sports in Kenya. This was followed by 

more bullish coverage

 of 

further investment

. What do we make of all this? What analytical language and tools do we have to observe and account for these significant on-ground events and dynamics?




One thing is clear: sports and commerce in East Africa are forming ever closer ties in countries such as Kenya and Uganda, across sectors, from rugby, boxing, basketball, and football to athletics, golf, badminton, and motocross, and, lately, e-sports. competitions

, events, teams, and

author: ROAPE
title: Mining in contemporary African underdevelopment
content:
One of the defining characteristics of capitalism is its remarkable ability to emerge from every crisis even stronger.[1] History has shown time and again that war and militarisation serve capitalism’s interests. And even in the case of the climate crisis – for which capitalism bears the greatest responsibility – we are presented with an alleged ‘win–win’ solution. While multinational companies at least partly withdraw from coal mining (see Tsuji et al. 2026, in this issue), the massive rise in 

demand for metals and minerals

 that are needed for ‘clean energy’, digitalisation, consumer electronics, aerospace and militarisation has led to a renewed mining boom, notably of so-called critical raw materials (UNCTAD 2026). In a business-as-usual scenario, demand for these materials between 2024 and 2040 is projected to increase by 353% in the case of lithium, 131% for graphite, 69% for nickel and 49% for cobalt (UNCTAD 2026, 3).




Many of the deposits of these raw materials are located in the global South, with the African continent accounting for about 30% of the world’s critical minerals and metals: for example, 85% of global deposits of manganese (in South Africa and Gabon) and 21% of graphite reserves (in Mozambique, Madagascar and Tanzania). author: ROAPE
title: Life after Museveni
content:
I have argued before that moving forward, Uganda will need General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, son of current President Yoweri Museveni. Or a person like Gen. Kainerugaba. This is not necessarily about the man, Muhoozi Kainerugaba. More that the trajectory of Museveni’s politics needs a man of this texture.




My intention here is neither support nor endorsement. But acknowledging Muhoozi’s usefulness in the transitional phase which must happen soon – or that is already underway.  Of course, his autocratic display thus far, is difficult to ignore.  But we have to acknowledge that Gen. Kainerugaba is a very important actor in an ongoing transition.




As 

the

 son of a sitting president, and current commander of the nation’s military, this is an unusual combination for anyone, and is therefore discussable on its merits. Especially with an octogenarian president, and a nervous country, surely this person – whoever they may be – is a key component.




I know, we are all running scared. Many comrades in the struggle for a good governance are still missing – Sam Mugumya. Many are rotting in jails and ‘safehouses’ across the country.  National Unity Platform (NUP)’s incarcerated supporters and leaders – Waiswa Mufumbiro, Eddie Mutwe, among others – are constantly threatened with public executions by the CDF himself, who is currently the president in waiting. We are all scared.

author: ROAPE
title: Bought, held, and sworn
content:
Somalia’s parliamentary election is not one election. It is 275 simultaneous, separate auctions. Each of Somalia’s 275 House of the People seats belongs to a specific sub-clan. Each is contested by a separate and distinct pool of delegates — assembled only for that seat, voting only on that seat, with no overlap with any other. What looks from outside like a single national election is, on the ground, 275 parallel closed markets operating at the same time — each with its own elder-broker, its own candidate payments, its own hotel rooms full of men who have been paid, sequestered, and made to swear on the Quran before they are allowed to vote. This is not electoral dysfunction. It is the operational logic of a system designed to convert clan identity and foreign financing into a self-reproducing governing class — one that controls parliament, elects the president, and uses both to block accountability for those who commit abuses in its service.




This investigation draws on primary source interviews with more than a dozen electoral delegates, parliamentary candidates, and traditional clan elders who participated directly in Somalia’s 2016–2017 and 2021–2022 parliamentary election cycles. It is corroborated by field research conducted by

author: ROAPE
title: Eusi Kwayana (1925-2026)
content:
Eusi Kwayana was born Sydney King, as he was known initially for his first, more than two decades in public life. In 1968 he took on his African name which in Swahili means ‘Black man of Guyana.’




Eusi Kwayana was a founding father of post-colonial independence Guyana and Caribbean politics and was associated with the triumvirate of personalities that shaped them: Cheddi Jagan, Forbes Burnham, and Walter Rodney. He came to write the anthems of the three parties they led. Yet his own contributions to the Black and global radical traditions are still being recognized and recorded. This will be challenging in an environment where he receives national and regional honors for being a mere educator, writer, and cultural activist. It’s undeniable; he was a revolutionary.




What does it mean that Eusi Kwayana was a revolutionary? He was a campaigner against white supremacy, empire, capitalism, patriarchy, and ecological destruction. More than that, where he led breakthroughs against colonialism that denied Guyana, the Caribbean, and the Global South self-government, at the post-colonial independence moment he continued to confront the African and Caribbean political class, whether aristocratic or progressive. author: ROAPE
title: African Labour and Liberation
content:
African Labour and Liberation

 brings together the experiences of workers, trade unions and labour movements across the continent to ask what they can tell us about work, power and liberation today. We assembled this collection because of the surprisingly few recent accounts of the emergence of a class politics on the continent. Labour is central to understanding the present political economy of Africa.  More than 90 percent of Africa’s 500 million workers work in informal and precarious jobs in a labour force that will grow rapidly in the next three decades.




The social and political mobilization of workers in multifarious contexts across the continent is imperative to improving their socio-economic conditions. It is necessary to situate Africa’s workers at the centre. This collection starts from the premise that labour struggles are essential to improving the conditions of work and stamping out poverty and inequality that the confronts most African workers today and form the basis for building new forms of collective power.




This heterodox collec­tion finds six primary patterns prevalent in the struggle for the working class liberation in the post-independence era.

author: ROAPE
title: Fanon’s continuing presence and revolutionary Sudan
content:
Each generation must out of relative obscurity discover its mission, fulfil it, or betray it.




– Frantz Fanon, 

The Wretched of the Earth

, 1968




I do not come with timeless truths … Every human problem must be considered from the standpoint of time.




– Frantz Fanon, 

Black Skin, White Masks

, 2008




 




Introduction




Fanon was very aware of his time. And yet one hundred years after his birth, he remains strangely present, as if we are repeating the same history, the long durée of the unfinished anticolonial revolutions (see Gibson 2021). Published in 1961, Fanon’s last book, 

The Wretched of the Earth

, is a product of his experience and reflections on Africa’s anticolonial struggle, including its first crisis in the Congo in 1961. Written as an intervention and addressing the readers as comrades, Fanon introduces the colonised challenge to the colonial world not as a rational confrontation of points of view, ‘but the untidy affirmation of an original idea propounded as an absolute’ (Fanon 1968, 41). Aware that colonialism carved up the continent into colonial fiefdoms, Fanon recognised that while the social struggle takes on a national form, it would inevitably degenerate into the regional, ethnic and racial lines often promulgated by colonial rule 

if

 it did not put into practice a ‘minimum humanist’ programme (Fanon 1968, 163).
